name: Harnessing technology to reach students during a pandemic

content.title: Harnessing technology to reach students during a pandemic
content.summary: AKU-SONAM EA shares the model for a successful blended learning approach

media.caption: AKU's Associate Registrar, East Africa takes students through the application process
media.alt: Harnessing technology to reach students during a pandemic

content.text: The Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery in East Africa (AKU-SONAM EA) held a Virtual Open Day on March 10, 2021, that hosted prospecting students from Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

The Open Day featured a seminar by the School's Academic Heads in the three countries titled "Advancing Nursing and Midwifery Education in East Africa: Harnessing Technology to Reach Everyone" as well as application information from the Aga Khan University's Office of the Registrar.

The seminar delved into how SONAM EA handled the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and encouraged students to join the School's blended learning programme. Speaking more on this, Dr Eunice Ndirangu-Mugo, Dean of SONAM EA shared that: "Due to our blended learning approach, learning transitioned fully online and we were able to continue providing our support to nurses and midwives in a time when they needed it most." Blended learning refers to an approach where education takes place partly online and also face-to-face. SONAM EA embraced this model several years ago to facilitate a work-study approach for nurses and midwives where they can immediately apply what they learn. The blended learning approach enables them valuable time on campus and guarantees more online interaction to allow them to meet their other work and family obligations.

The seminar was the backbone of the Virtual Open Day as it enabled prospecting students to understand how the School adapted learning for frontline healthcare workers as well as ask questions on this important aspect of current learning. SONAM's Academic Head in Uganda, Joseph Mwizerwa assured students that the School's Virtual learning platform had been established several years ago and the pandemic only served to shift learning fully online. He added: "A month after the lock-down in Uganda (and Kenya), all learning was restructured to Moodle, our Virtual Learning platform and students continued learning. We trained faculty on full use of the platform and oriented students on the use of Zoom as well as provided data bundles to faculty, staff and students."

In Tanzania, the COVID protocols were slightly different however faculty and students still maintained institutionally-approved AKU guidelines. Regardless, Dr Eunice Siaity, Academic Head in SONAM Tanzania noted: "Initially, it was difficult to believe that a course could end without interacting with our students face-to-face but synchronized lectures on Zoom helped a lot. As our students were at the forefront of the pandemic, the need for closer communication became necessary. Faculty were receiving more calls and requests for live chats from students more frequently so that they could seek clarity easily. Unexpectedly, all this strengthened our relationship with our students."
Thereafter, there was a session where students engaged with the Registrar's Office about application procedures, student life and other aspects that shed more light on education during COVID times.

Among the over 80 attendees were a few current students who were looking to appreciate the registrars and faculty for their good work throughout the pandemic. Among them was Isaac from SONAM Uganda who was happy to have learned at SONAM, mentioning: "When applying, I missed my scheduled interview. Gladys, the registrar, ensured I was interviewed later on and now, I am set to graduate with a degree in Nursing in December. Thank you!" Another student, Carolyne Ndungu, from the Advanced Practice Nursing Masters was really happy about how the School and the Library partnered to ensure learning continued. She said, "The IT team would always pick our calls and address our concerns whenever we called, and the Library made so much reading material available online which made learning so easy."

Despite the pandemic, the Aga Khan University School of Nursing and Midwifery embraced a learning approach which ensured that all educational aspects shifted online and nurses and midwives were still able to connect with faculty in moments when healthcare systems needed them the most.
